newsitem.title: INDIA: Profiles of possible successors to Mother Teresa.
newsitem.headline: Profiles of possible successors to Mother Teresa.

text.p: Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity religious order is expected to elect a successor to lead the Roman Catholic order any day now.
The balloting to find a successor to the ailing 86-year-old charismatic nun was originally scheduled for September 8 last year but has been postponed twice due to her poor health.
Roman Catholic rules stipulate that the superior general of any order can be elected for a maximum of six years and can be re-elected for one more term.

But successive popes made an exception for Mother Teresa, who founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1948 in the eastern Indian city of Calcutta. In past elections Mother Teresa has won all the votes -- except her own.
This time she has asked to step down due to poor health.
Any sister of the order who has completed at least five years after her final vows is eligible to run.
Three councillors general -- Sisters Frederick, Joseph Michael and Priscilla Lewis -- and another senior nun, Sister Nirmala, are considered the front-runners.
The Vatican has no direct influence on the vote, but it ratifies the final choice. The election process involves the 132 members of the order's electoral order, or the General Chapter.
Mother Teresa never groomed a successor. Her replacement is expected to try to make up in administrative ability what she may lack in charisma compared to the Nobel Peace Prize winner.

SISTER FREDERICK - The most senior of the four councillors-general -- she won the maximum number of votes in 1990 to the governing council -- she is considered a strict disciplinarian and hard worker. The 81-year-old Anglo-Maltese nun has recently been very close to Mother Teresa, and is in charge of her medical treatment. In the past the publicity-shy nun was responsible for the order's United States operations.

SISTER JOSEPH MICHAEL - Educated at the Loreto Convent in Calcutta, she was Mother Teresa's secretary until she became a councillor-general. She keeps a low profile and is in charge of training the sisters. The Press Trust of India said Mother Teresa had in the past voted for Sister Joseph Michael to succeed her.

SISTER PRISCILLA LEWIS - An Anglo-Indian former school teacher from the northeastern state of Meghalaya, she has been the spokeswoman for the order during a period when its fund-raising and opposition to birth control have been criticised. She worked as a missionary in New York for 16 years. In her early 60s, she determines Mother Teresa's schedule and whom she should meet.

SISTER NIRMALA - A Hindu convert, she has supervised the order's centres in Europe and the United States. She heads the order's contemplative wing, in which elite nuns dedicate their lives to meditation. Considered a dark horse, she is not one of the four councillors-general, but the order's constitution allows her to be elevated to superior general.

SISTER AGNES DAS - Aged 66, she was one of Mother Teresa's first helpers. Mother Teresa gave Das her name Agnes and has described her as her "second self". In 1990, when Mother Teresa wanted to step down on health grounds, Sister Agnes Das also withdrew her name on medical grounds. A Bengali by birth, she has health problems which some believe could hamper her chances.

SISTER ANDREAS BOENKE - She studied medicine at Calcutta Medical College and has worked in the Philippines. Her good international contacts and the key role she has played in developing the order's global thrust are potential advantages.
